content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a novel graph contrastive learning method named GraphCV to learn representation from graph data.  The main purpose of GraphCV is to distinguish between the predictive and other non-predictive features. In particular, the authors introduce a cross-view reconstruction mechanism for the purpose. Furthermore, an adversarial view is further added as the third view for the contrastive loss to ensure the global semantics and improve the representation robustness. The authors provide theoretical analysis on the proposed model designs. Comprehensive experiments on multiple graph benchmark datasets are conducted. The results show GraphCV outperforms existing methods and is able to learn robust and transferable graph representations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
•	The authors propose a novel method to alleviate the feature suppression issue. A cross-view reconstruction mechanism is introduced to disentangle different learned representations.
•	The presentation is clear and experimental results are clearly discussed and analysed.
Weaknesses:
•	The novelty of this paper might be slightly insufficient. My understanding is that the proposed model can be considered as an extension of previous GraphCL. Despite the introduction of cross-view reconstruction, it seems that cross-view reconstruction exists in previous graph representation learning studies. 
•	The performance might be still somewhat limited. The authors compared many methods under different settings with GraphCV on multiple datasets. However, it can be found that GraphCV is comparable to or even underperforms the best baseline in many cases. While GraphCV has better performance than baselines in some cases, the advantages are not significant enough.
Other questions:
•	Why are two data augmentation graphs needed?
•	The proposed model is involved in multiple losses. How to determine the weight values of different losses? Could the fixed weight values be generalized to different datasets?

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work considers the graph representation learning problems, where the focus is to solve the feature suppression issue in the graph contrastive learning method. To achieve this, a new method that used a cross-view reconstruction technique is proposed. To show the effectiveness of the proposed method, some theoretical support and empirical evaluations are provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This work is technically sound, to show the effectiveness of the proposed method, both theoretical analyses and empirical evaluations are provided. Besides, some nice graphs about the proposed framework are given to help the readers understand paper. However, this work can be further improved in the following aspects:

- Some figures are not vector graphs, for example, fig. 3 and fig. 4. These should be revised.
- The proofs in the Appendix should be further polished. There are a lot of typos. For instance, there exists an extra equal sign in equation (12), and equation (10) misses a period.
- It would be better to have some discussions and explanations about the major theorems, like why these theorems are needed and how these theorems can guarantee that the proposed algorithm works well.
- This paper is not well-organized. The organization is kind of messy and not easy to follow. For example, in both Sec. 1 and Sec. 5, the related works are discussed. It would be better to incorporate these sections together. Also, it would be better to put the theoretical analyses into a separate section rather than listed in a subsection of the model.
- Can you compare the proposed model with other graph contrastive learning methods in depth?
- This paper was published on arxiv (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.07699.pdf) with the header showing that “it is published as a conference paper at ICLR 2023”. This might violate the double-blind review requirement.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors introduce Graph Contrastive Learning with Cross-View Reconstruction (GraphCV), which follows the information bottleneck principle to learn minimal yet sufficient representation from graph data. Besides, an adversarial view perturbed from the original view is added as the third view for the contrastive loss to guarantee the intactness of the global semantics and improve the representation robustness. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The idea of the proposed method is easy to follow and effective.

2. The experiments and analysis are sufficient. 

3. The theoretical analysis is solid and improves the quality of this paper.

Weaknesses:
1. The existing problems are not specific, and the motivation is unclear enough. The authors need to specifically claim the problems in the existing methods and how the proposed method can solve them in a few sentences.

2. The novelty of adversarial view generation is limited. It has been proposed in many papers [1, 2]. The authors should detail the differences.

3. I suggest the authors should demonstrate the phenomenon in Figure 1 with extensive experiments.

4. There is something wrong in Table 2. For example, on SIDER dataset, there are two bolded numbers, and on Clin Tox dataset, there is no underlined numbers.


[1] Susheel Suresh, Pan Li, Cong Hao, and Jennifer Neville. Adversarial Graph Augmentation to Improve Graph Contrastive Learning. In NeurIPS, 2021.

[2] Longqi Yang, Liangliang Zhang, and Wenjing Yang. Graph Adversarial Self-Supervised Learning. In NeurIPS, 2021.

content.title: Contrastive Graph Representation Learning with Cross-view Reconstruction
content.TL;DR: Our paper propose a new contrastive learning framework to learn graph representation in accordance with the information bottleneck principle.
content.abstract: Although different graph self-supervised learning strategies have been proposed to tackle the supervision shortage issue in graph learning tasks, Graph contrastive learning (GCL) has been the most prevalent approach to this problem.  Despite the remarkable performances those GCL methods have achieved, existing GCL methods that heavily depend on various manually designed augmentation techniques still struggle to improve model robustness without risking losing task-relevant information. Consequently, the learned representation is either brittle or unilluminating. In light of this, we introduce the GraphCV, which follows the information bottleneck principle to learn minimal yet sufficient representations from graph data. Specifically, our proposed model elicits the predictive (useful for downstream instance discrimination) and other non-predictive features separately. Except for the conventional contrastive loss which guarantees the consistency and sufficiency of the representations across different augmentation views, we introduce a cross-view reconstruction mechanism to pursue the disentanglement of the two learned representations. Besides, an adversarial global view is added as the third view of contrastive loss to avoid the learned representation from being drafted too far away from the original distribution. We empirically demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms the state-of-the-art on graph classification task over multiple benchmark datasets.
